results.result: mRNAs encoding secreted proteins involved in yeast mating (pheromones, pheromone receptors, agglutinins) multiplex in trans to form functionally selective mRNP complexes called 'mating transperons' in both MATα and MATa cell types. This was demonstrated through RaPID-seq and RaPID-qPCR experiments showing co-precipitation of specific mating pathway mRNAs.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C15, C16, C32, C34, C36, C38, and C97 collectively demonstrate mRNA multiplexing through multiple independent experimental approaches (RaPID-seq in Figure 1, RaPID-qPCR in Figure 2A-B). The specificity is shown by negative enrichment of opposite mating-type RNAs (C35) and lack of co-precipitation of unrelated mRNAs (C36). The data consistently support the existence of mating transperons across both mating types.

results.result: Mating pathway mRNAs co-localize to the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) in the cell body, both in the nucleus and cytoplasm, with or without pheromone treatment. Quantitative co-localization analysis showed 65.5-73.1% co-localization between STE2 and AGA2 mRNAs, and 37.9% between AGA1 and STE2 mRNAs, while control mRNA HSP150 showed only 9.8% co-localization with STE2.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C44 are supported by multiple imaging approaches including confocal microscopy (Figure 2C-D), live cell imaging (Figure 2D), and smFISH (Figure 2E-F, Figure 3A-B). The quantitative data show statistically significant co-localization of mating mRNAs with appropriate negative controls (C44), and the localization to ER rather than bud/shmoo tips is clearly demonstrated.

results.result: Histone H4 paralogs (Hhf1 and Hhf2) specifically interact with mating transperon mRNAs. A ~150 kDa band identified by RaPID-MS contained Hhf1, and HA-Hhf1 immunoprecipitation specifically pulled down mating mRNAs (STE2, MFA1, MFA2) but not control mRNAs (EXO70, ASH1, SRO7, UBC6).
results.evaluation: Claims C17, C45-C49 are well-supported by RaPID-MS identification (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), immunoprecipitation with RT-PCR (Figure 3C), Western blot showing expected molecular weight (Figure 3D), and qRT-PCR validation (Figure 3E). The specificity of H4-mRNA interaction is demonstrated by negative controls showing no binding to unrelated mRNAs.

results.result: Histone H4 is required for mating transperon assembly. Deletion of HHF1 or HHF2 led to 50-60% reduction in mating efficiency, and auxin-induced depletion of Hhf1 resulted in >80% inhibition of mating, reduced mRNA co-localization (from 37.9% to 14-15.9%), and decreased co-precipitation of mating mRNAs by ~50%.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C5, C50-C52, C54-C56 are supported by multiple complementary experiments: quantitative mating assays (Figure 4A-B), Western blots confirming H4 depletion (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), smFISH showing reduced co-localization (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E), and RaPID-qPCR demonstrating reduced mRNA multiplexing (Figure 4C-D). The auxin-inducible degron system provides temporal control validating the requirement.

results.result: Histone H4 acetylation is required for mating. Only H4 deletions (not other histones) significantly reduced mating, deletion of histone acetyltransferases HAT1 or SAS2 reduced mating efficiency, K-to-R mutations (blocking acetylation) abolished mating enhancement, while K-to-Q mutations (mimicking acetylation) increased mating 2-fold like wild-type H4 overexpression.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C18, C19, C57-C61 are supported by systematic analysis of histone deletions (Figure 4A), HAT deletion studies (Figure 5A), and acetylation mutant analysis (Figure 5B-C). The specificity for H4 (C19) and the opposing effects of K-to-R versus K-to-Q mutations provide strong evidence for the importance of H4 acetylation in mating.

results.result: A conserved 47-nucleotide motif in the coding region of MATa mating mRNAs is required for transperon assembly and mating. Mutation of this motif in AGA2 (AGA2 47-MUT but not AGA2 27-MUT) led to loss of AGA2 mRNA assembly into the mating mRNP and significant defects in mating efficiency.
results.evaluation: Claims C20, C21, C65-C67 are supported by MEME bioinformatic analysis identifying the motif (Figure 6A), RaPID-qPCR showing loss of multiplexing with the 47-nucleotide mutation (Figure 6B), and quantitative mating assays demonstrating functional consequences (Figure 6C). The differential effects of 27-MUT versus 47-MUT provide specificity.

results.result: The STE2 and AGA2 genes physically interact through intergenic chromatin associations. Chromatin conformation capture identified three specific interactions (ORF-ORF, ORF-5'UTR, 3'UTR-3'UTR), and live cell imaging showed 83.1% of loci were either fully co-localized (9.5%) or adjacent (73.6%), compared to only 29.5% for the control AGA2-ASH1 pair.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C22, C73-C77 are supported by chromatin conformation capture (3C) experiments with DNA sequencing confirmation (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A-B) and live cell fluorescence microscopy of tagged genomic loci (Figure 7C, Figure 7—figure supplement 1C-D). The specificity is demonstrated by negative controls showing minimal interaction between non-multiplexing genes.

results.result: Allelic coupling between mating genes is transcription- and histone H4-dependent. Treatment with transcription inhibitor 1,10-phenanthroline increased non-co-localized alleles by 40-50%, and HHF1 deletion reduced allelic coupling, suggesting H4 has a structural role in mediating intergenic interactions that lead to RNA multiplexing.
results.evaluation: Claims C23, C78, C79, C98-C100 are supported by live cell imaging experiments with transcription inhibitor (Figure 7—figure supplement 1E) and in hhf1Δ cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 1F). However, the mechanistic interpretation (C98-C100) involves speculation about causality. The data show correlation between allelic coupling and RNA multiplexing but do not definitively prove the former causes the latter.

results.result: Heat shock protein (HSP) mRNAs multiplex in trans during heat shock to form RNP complexes. HSP104 and SSA2 mRNA co-localization increased from 30.4% under non-heat shock to 76.8% upon heat shock, while control STE2-SSA2 co-localization remained low (~11-12%) regardless of heat shock.
results.evaluation: Claims C25, C80-C82 are supported by RaPID-qPCR showing increased co-precipitation of HSP mRNAs after heat shock (Figure 8A) and smFISH demonstrating increased co-localization (Figure 8B-C). The specificity is shown by the control comparison with STE2 mRNA (C82), and the data are consistent with prior work on HSP gene intergenic interactions (C24).

results.result: Histone H4 is required for HSP mRNA multiplexing and post-heat shock cell recovery. H4 depletion reduced HSP mRNA co-precipitation and co-localization (from 76.8% to 51.5-55.8%), and AID-HHF1 hhf2Δ cells treated with auxin showed longer doubling times after heat shock compared to wild-type or untreated cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C26, C84-C87 are supported by RaPID-qPCR in H4-depleted cells (Figure 8—figure supplement 2A-B), smFISH showing reduced co-localization (Figure 8—figure supplement 2C), and growth assays demonstrating physiological consequences (Figure 8—figure supplement 1D). The data parallel the mating transperon results, strengthening the general role of H4 in transperon assembly.

results.result: Additional RNA multiplexes exist for mitochondrial outer membrane proteins (MOMPs) and MAP kinase pathway proteins. UGO1 mRNA co-precipitated with MOMP mRNAs (TOM5, TOM6, TOM22) and showed 46.3% co-localization with TOM6 by smFISH. STE5 mRNA co-precipitated with FUS3 mRNA and showed 19.6% co-localization, while controls showed <8% co-localization.
results.evaluation: Claims C27, C88-C94 are supported by RaPID-qPCR (Figure 9A, D) and smFISH (Figure 9B-C, E-F) with appropriate negative controls. However, the MOMP and MAPK multiplexes show lower co-localization percentages than mating or HSP transperons, and the MAPK data show only slight increases for STE7/STE11 (C92), suggesting these may be weaker or more transient interactions.

results.result: HHF1 and SCP160 work cooperatively but non-epistatically in mating. Crosses of hhf1Δ × scp160Δ showed similar mating defects to hhf1Δ × WT, but hhf1Δ scp160Δ double mutants were completely sterile. Auxin treatment did not abolish pheromone-induced increases in mating mRNA levels.
results.evaluation: Claims C53, C62-C64 are supported by quantitative mating assays (Figure 5D), qRT-PCR showing maintained pheromone response (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D), and citation to prior work on SCP160 (C62). The genetic interaction data suggest HHF1 and SCP160 function in parallel pathways that both contribute to mating, though the complete sterility of the double mutant requires further mechanistic explanation.

results.result: P-body components are not required for mating under normal growth conditions. Deletion of DHH1, PAT1, or both had no significant effect on mating. Under normal glucose conditions, few cells (2.3%) had P-body puncta and showed little mRNA co-localization, but glucose starvation induced P-body formation and 40.9% co-localization with STE2 mRNA.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C72 are supported by quantitative mating assays (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B) and confocal microscopy (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C). This contradicts prior published work (Aronov et al., 2015) but is consistent with the authors' previous findings (Haimovich et al., 2016). The data suggest P-bodies form under stress but are not sites of mating mRNA localization under normal conditions.

results.result: Conserved sequence motifs exist in transperon mRNAs. Two distinct motifs of 45 and 25 bases were identified in MATα mating mRNAs (MFα1, MFα2, STE3, SAG1), and three motifs were identified in HSP gene sequences present in nearly all HSP cohort genes.
results.evaluation: Claims C68 and C83 are supported by MEME bioinformatic analysis (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C, Figure 8—figure supplement 1A-B). However, unlike the MATa motif (C65-C67), these motifs were not functionally validated through mutagenesis experiments, so their role in transperon assembly remains uncertain. The identification is descriptive rather than mechanistic.

results.result: Background claims about prokaryotic operons, eukaryotic gene organization, and RNA-binding proteins establish the scientific context. Prokaryotes use polycistronic operons, while eukaryotes have limited examples (C. elegans). Eukaryotic mRNPs contain multiple RNAs and RBPs, genomic DNA folds create transcriptional hot spots, and extensive RNA-RNA interactions occur in living cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C9-C13 are background knowledge claims supported by appropriate citations to published literature. These establish the conceptual framework for the study but do not represent novel findings. They are accurately stated and properly referenced.

results.result: The RaPID method allows biochemical analysis of mRNP composition at single transcript level. RaPID-seq identifies MS2-tagged target mRNAs and co-precipitated non-tagged RNAs including retrotransposable elements, tRNAs, ribosomal RNAs, and coding RNAs. Target transcripts included cER-localized mRNAs encoding polarity factors (SRO7, EXO70) and mitochondrial outer membrane protein OM45.
results.evaluation: Claims C14, C29-C31, C33 describe the RaPID methodology and initial observations. These are supported by citations to prior work (C14, C29, C30) and data in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1 (C31). The characterization of target transcripts (C33) is supported by citations to previous publications. These are methodological and descriptive claims that set up the main findings.

results.result: The authors propose that intergenic associations and non-canonical histone H4 functions contribute to transperon formation in eukaryotic cells to regulate cell physiology. They suggest eukaryotes circumvent polycistronicity by assembling mRNAs into functional complexes via physical intergenic interactions concurrent with transcription, and that transperons are functional equivalents of bacterial operons.
results.evaluation: Claims C8, C28, C95-C96, C101-C103 are speculative proposals and interpretations based on the experimental data. While the data support RNA multiplexing, H4 involvement, and intergenic interactions, the mechanistic model of how these processes are coordinated and the claim that transperons are 'functional equivalents' of operons involve significant inference beyond what is directly demonstrated. The model is plausible but requires additional validation.
